source: The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight. As it goes around the Earth, about once a month, we see more or less of its sunlit half: new, crescent, quarter, gibbous and full.
Thinking the Earth's shadow makes the phases. The shadow only matters in an eclipse; phases come from how much of the Moon's lit half faces us.
Some nights the Moon is a round, bright ball. Some nights it is a thin smile. Some nights you cannot see it at all. The Moon has not changed shape; we see different amounts of its lit half.

The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight. One half of it is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon travels around the Earth, about once every 29½ days, we see more or less of that lit half. These are the phases.
The phases of the Moon, in order: new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.
Waxing means growing (more lit each night); waning means shrinking. Gibbous means more than half lit.
Tonight is a full moon. What phase will it be in about one week?
About a week after full comes the last quarter.
Thinking the Earth's shadow makes the phases. The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which happens only now and then, about twice a year.
